title: Should Christians Ever Go to War?
excerpt: Jesus told his followers to love their enemies and put away the sword, his church has prayed over armies for sixteen hundred years, and Christians who take both facts seriously have come to two different answers and one shared shame.
body:
Three people can hear the word war in the same church and hear three different things. One wore a uniform for twenty years and has never told anyone in the congregation what he saw, or what he did, because he does not know which he fears more, their admiration or their questions. One is eighteen and deciding whether to enlist, and has heard a hundred sermons on loving her enemies and not one on what a Christian does with a rifle. One belongs to a family that has refused to carry weapons for four hundred years, and has been called a coward by people who never asked what that refusal cost her grandfather.

The skeptic watching them has a strong charge to bring. Jesus told his followers to love their enemies and to put away the sword. His church has since prayed over nearly every army that asked, often over both armies in the same war. A religion that can do that, the skeptic says, is following whoever happens to be in command, and its founder is not the one in command.

Most of that charge is true. And if you have carried a weapon and carry something heavier now, hear one thing before the argument starts. If you have started to wonder whether you want to go on living, reach out today: in the US, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. [Find Help](/help) has other lines you can call.

## What Jesus Said, and What Paul Said

The hard words are in the Sermon on the Mount. "You have heard that it was said, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.' But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Matthew 5:38–39). A few sentences later: "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 5:44–45). The reason he gives is God's own character: the Father sends rain on the just and the unjust.

Jesus kept his own teaching. On the night of his arrest one of his disciples drew a sword and cut off the ear of a servant in the arresting party. "Put your sword back into its place," Jesus told him. "For all who take the sword will perish by the sword" (Matthew 26:52). Luke adds that he said, "No more of this!" (Luke 22:51), and that he healed the man's ear. The next morning he told the Roman governor, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36).

Paul writes in the same key. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'" (Romans 12:19). Then, with no break in the letter, he turns to the governing authority. The ruler "does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4). The Christian is told never to take vengeance. A few lines later the ruler is called God's servant for carrying it out.

The debate turns on how those two paragraphs fit together. One reading says Paul is describing two different sets of people: the church, which does not avenge, and the state, which God uses in spite of itself. The other says he is describing two roles that one person may hold, forgiving his own enemies as a private man and protecting his neighbors as a public one.

The New Testament also shows soldiers, and it treats them with respect. When soldiers asked John the Baptist what repentance meant for them, he said, "Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages" (Luke 3:14). Jesus said of a Roman centurion, "with no one in Israel have I found such faith" (Matthew 8:10). The first Gentile baptized in the book of Acts was another centurion, Cornelius, "a devout man who feared God with all his household" (Acts 10:2). None of them is told to leave the army. None of them is told he may kill, either. Both sides have built on that silence.

## The First Three Centuries

For its first three centuries the church had no armies to pray over, and the Christian teachers who took up the question answered it one way.

Tertullian, writing in Carthage in North Africa in the years around 200, asked whether a believer could be a soldier at all. "But how will a Christian man war," he wrote, "nay, how will he serve even in peace, without a sword, which the Lord has taken away?" In another book he asked, "Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword?" The pagan critic Celsus had urged Christians to take up arms for the emperor. When Origen of Alexandria, among the most learned Christians of the third century, wrote his reply, he did not pretend that they would. "We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it," Origen answered, "but we fight on his behalf," by which he meant prayer.

The record has to be read whole. Tertullian himself, defending Christians to the Roman public, reminded them that "We sail with you, and fight with you, and till the ground with you," so there were Christians in the legions when he wrote. Part of his objection to the army was its idolatry, the oaths and sacrifices that came with the camp. And Origen, in the same passage, speaks of praying for "those who are fighting in a righteous cause." Historians still argue over how much of the early refusal was about bloodshed and how much was about idols. What the books leave beyond argument is that the church's first teachers thought the sword and the disciple did not belong together.

The conviction outlived the persecutions. Martin, a soldier in Gaul in the fourth century and later the bishop of Tours, asked for his discharge on the eve of a battle. His biographer gives his words to the commander: "I am the soldier of Christ" and "it is not lawful for me to fight." Accused of cowardice, he offered to stand unarmed in front of the line the next morning.

## Augustine and the Just War

Then the emperor became a Christian. Constantine won the western empire in 312, and within a century the men responsible for defending the frontiers were baptized. The question was no longer whether a Christian could serve a pagan emperor. It was what a Christian ruler owed to the people the invaders were killing.

Augustine, the bishop of Hippo in North Africa, gave the answer that most of the church has lived by since. He wrote in the years after Rome itself was sacked, in 410. In 418 he sent a letter to a Roman commander named Boniface, whose work was fighting the peoples Augustine calls the barbarians. "Do not think," he told him, "that it is impossible for any one to please God while engaged in active military service." Then he set the terms: "Peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity."

That sounds like permission, and Augustine meant it as a restraint. "The real evils in war," he wrote elsewhere, "are love of violence, revengeful cruelty, fierce and implacable enmity, wild resistance, and the lust of power." A war fought with those in the heart was sin even if the cause was right. And in *The City of God* he refused to let anyone feel clean about it. People say the wise man will wage just wars, he wrote. "As if he would not all the rather lament the necessity of just wars, if he remembers that he is a man."

Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, gave the teaching the form in which it was handed on. "In order for a war to be just," he wrote in the *Summa Theologiae*, "three things are necessary." The first is "the authority of the sovereign," because no private person may declare war. The second is "a just cause," which he defined as a real wrong done by those attacked. The third is "a rightful intention," the aim of doing good or preventing evil, since a war "declared by the legitimate authority, and for a just cause" can still be made wrong "through a wicked intention." Later teachers added that every peaceful means be tried first, that the harm done not outweigh the good sought, and that those who are not fighting never be made targets.

In its own terms the just war teaching is an act of love. Its defenders begin where Jesus does, with the neighbor. If a man is beating a child in the street, the one who loves them both stops him, by force if nothing else will do. A ruler stands in that street for a whole people. The teaching says that a fallen world sometimes offers only a choice between evils, and it gives the conscience a list of questions meant to be answered no far more often than yes. A war that fails them is unjust killing, and the teaching holds that a Christian must not fight in it. The Protestant confessions kept this teaching. The Lutheran confession of 1530 says that Christians may "engage in just wars" and "serve as soldiers."

## The Church That Refused

The Lutheran article goes on to its next sentence: "They condemn the Anabaptists who forbid these civil offices to Christians."

The Anabaptists were the Reformation's third party, the believers in Zurich and southern Germany who concluded in the 1520s that a church is made of people who have chosen to follow Christ and that such people do not kill. In February 1527 a group of them met at Schleitheim, on the Swiss border, and agreed on seven articles drafted around a former prior named Michael Sattler. The sixth concerns the sword, and it is more careful than its enemies allowed: "The sword is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ," it says. "It punishes and puts to death the wicked, and guards and protects the good." The Anabaptists did not say that governments have no right to exist. They said that the Christian has been called to a different work. Sattler was tortured and burned within months. Catholic and Protestant governments alike hunted Anabaptists for a century, and the descendants of the survivors, Mennonites and Amish among them, have kept the conviction ever since.

In its own terms the pacifist case is a claim about what Jesus commanded and how God wins, and only secondly a hope of making wars stop. Jesus did not say to love enemies when it is safe. He said it to people under military occupation, and then he went to a cross when he could have called on legions. The church, on this view, is the one people on earth whose members are found in every nation, and when Christians kill for their countries they kill each other. The martyrs in Revelation conquer "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death" (Revelation 12:11). The pacifist believes that this is the only kind of victory a Christian has been promised.

Each side has a question it finds hard. The pacifist is asked what he would have the strong do while the weak are slaughtered, and whether it is honest to live safely behind soldiers and police whose work he calls forbidden. He answers that obedience was never promised to be safe, and that his people have accepted prison and death for it. The just war Christian is asked how often, in sixteen centuries, his list of questions has led a church to tell its own nation no. He is asked how he reads Matthew 5 without making it mean nothing.

## When We Called War Holy

There is a third thing in Christian history, and neither side claims it. In 1095, at Clermont in France, Pope Urban II preached an armed pilgrimage to recover Jerusalem and offered remission of penance to those who went. The chroniclers record the crowd's answer: God wills it. Before the armies had left Europe, crusading bands massacred the Jewish communities of the Rhineland, at Worms and Mainz, in 1096. When Jerusalem fell in 1099 the crusaders slaughtered its people, Muslim and Jewish alike. In 1204 a crusade turned aside and sacked the Christian city of Constantinople.

Augustine had said that war was a necessity to be lamented. The crusade said that war was a holy work, that the enemy was God's enemy, and that killing him was good for the soul. That was a different teaching. Seven centuries before Urban, Basil of Caesarea had written that the fathers did not count killing in war as murder, and had still advised that soldiers "whose hands are not clean" should "abstain from communion for three years." A church that once kept its own soldiers from the table for a time now sent them out with a promise of pardon.

We have not left that habit behind. It appears whenever we speak of our country's enemies as God's enemies, whenever a pulpit hands out certainty about a war that it has not weighed by any test at all, and whenever the dead on the other side are left out of the prayers. Christians who hold the just war teaching should be the first to say so, because it is their teaching that the crusade wears as a costume. Another essay on this site takes up [what happens when a nation is called Christian](/writing/can-a-nation-be-christian).

## The Lion Who Is a Lamb

Both sides appeal to the last book of the Bible. In John's vision an elder tells him to stop weeping, because "the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered" (Revelation 5:5). John turns to look at the Lion. What he sees is "a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain" (Revelation 5:6). The conqueror has won by being killed, and from that point on the book's name for him is the Lamb.

Near the end he rides out to judge the nations. He wears "a robe dipped in blood" before any battle has been fought, and the only weapon named is the sword that comes "from his mouth" (Revelation 19:13, 15). Christians who refuse war read this as the Lamb still conquering by his own blood and his own word. Christians who accept it under limits point out that the judgment is real, and that Paul gave it as the reason to leave vengeance alone. On either reading, the final violence in history belongs to Christ and to no one else, and no nation's cause is his.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess together that Jesus Christ is Lord of every ruler and every nation, that human beings are made in God's image and that murder is a grave evil, that enemies are to be loved and prayed for, that vengeance belongs to God, and that the kingdom of God does not come by the sword. They confess that Christ will come to judge and that a day is coming when the nations "shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks" (Isaiah 2:4). No Christian tradition today teaches that war is good in itself.

Whether a Christian may bear arms for the state under strict limits, or must refuse, is a question of the second order. The larger part of the church has held the first answer since Augustine. A smaller part, with the earliest Christian teachers behind it, has held the second, and has often paid for it. This essay has set the two side by side and does not choose between them.

Whether any particular war meets the tests is a judgment no page can make, and this one names none.

The church has reason to honor two people it has usually set against each other. One is the objector who went to prison, or carried a stretcher under fire with no weapon, because he believed Jesus meant what he said. The other is the soldier who went because he believed that love of his neighbor required it, and the chaplain who went with him, unarmed, to be near the dying. What the church owes them both is the truth, and it has given too little of it. It has called the first a coward. It has sent the second off with flags and received him home with applause, and has not asked what the killing did to him, as Basil's generation knew to ask.

On the night Jesus was arrested, the last thing he did before his hands were bound was to heal a wound that one of his own disciples had made with a sword. The man he healed had come to arrest him. Every Christian who puts on a uniform, and every Christian who refuses one, has to give an account of that garden. The promise that the nations will not "learn war anymore" (Isaiah 2:4) has not yet been kept, and until it is, neither the one who fights nor the one who refuses gets to be at ease.

*"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God."* (Matthew 5:9)

*"He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore."* (Isaiah 2:4)
